# Pathophysiology of Obesity

## Central Regulation of Energy Balance

The maintenance of body weight is governed by a tightly integrated neuroendocrine system
centred on the arcuate nucleus (ARC) of the hypothalamus, which functions as the primary
integrator of peripheral satiety and adiposity signals. Within the ARC, two anatomically
interdigitated but functionally antagonistic neuronal populations exert opposing influences on
energy homeostasis. Neuropeptide Y (NPY) and agouti-related peptide (AgRP) co-expressing
neurons are potently orexigenic: when activated — as occurs during caloric deficit or low
leptin states — they release NPY acting via Y1 and Y5 receptors to stimulate food intake, and
AgRP, which functions as an endogenous inverse agonist at the melanocortin-4 receptor (MC4R),
blocking the anorexigenic melanocortin signalling cascade. Opposing these are the pro-opiomelanocortin
(POMC) and cocaine- and amphetamine-regulated transcript (CART) co-expressing neurons, which
are anorexigenic: POMC undergoes post-translational cleavage by prohormone convertase 1/3
(PC1/3) to yield α-melanocyte-stimulating hormone (α-MSH), which binds MC4R in the
paraventricular nucleus (PVN) to reduce food intake and increase energy expenditure
[@Muller2022Antiobesity; @Bluher2019Obesity].

MC4R occupies a position of singular importance in human obesity genetics. Loss-of-function
variants in the *MC4R* gene are identified in approximately 2–6% of individuals with severe
obesity, constituting the most common monogenic cause of common obesity [@Muller2022Antiobesity].
The receptor signals primarily via Gαs-coupled adenylyl cyclase activation, but also
recruits β-arrestin pathways that modulate receptor internalisation and downstream MAPK
signalling. The upstream regulator of this axis is leptin, a 16-kDa adipokine encoded by the
*LEP* gene and secreted proportionally to adipose tissue mass. Leptin traverses the blood–brain
barrier via a saturable transport mechanism and binds the long-form leptin receptor (LEPRb) on
ARC POMC neurons, activating JAK2–STAT3 phosphorylation and driving *Pomc* gene transcription
[@Fasshauer2015Adipokines]. In the obese state, despite dramatically elevated circulating
leptin concentrations — commonly exceeding 30–40 ng/mL compared with 5–10 ng/mL in lean
individuals — central leptin resistance emerges through multiple mechanisms including
downregulation of LEPRb expression, impaired JAK2 signalling secondary to suppressor of
cytokine signalling-3 (SOCS3) induction, and reduced leptin transport across the blood–brain
barrier. This functional leptin resistance effectively uncouples adiposity from the
homeostatic braking mechanisms that should limit further weight gain, creating a permissive
neurobiological environment for progressive obesity.

## The Gut–Brain Axis: Incretin and Satiety Hormones

The gastrointestinal tract functions as the body's largest endocrine organ and is an essential
afferent limb of the gut–brain energy-sensing axis. Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1) is
derived from the *GCG* gene product proglucagon through differential post-translational
processing in intestinal L-cells concentrated in the distal ileum and colon; in contrast,
pancreatic α-cells process the same proglucagon precursor to yield glucagon [@Holst2007Physiology;
@Drucker2018Mechanisms]. Following nutrient ingestion, L-cells secrete GLP-1 into the portal
circulation within minutes; GLP-1 then acts through multiple mechanisms to reduce energy intake:
it slows gastric emptying, augments glucose-stimulated insulin secretion from pancreatic
β-cells, suppresses glucagon secretion from α-cells, and — crucially for obesity pharmacotherapy —
activates GLP-1 receptors (GLP-1R) on vagal afferent neurons innervating the hepatoportal
region and nodose ganglion, transmitting satiety signals to the nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS)
in the brainstem, which in turn relays these signals to hypothalamic centres [@Muller2019Glucagon].
GLP-1R are also expressed directly on ARC neurons, providing a direct central pathway for
GLP-1-mediated appetite suppression.

Glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), secreted from K-cells of the proximal
small intestine in response to fat and carbohydrate ingestion, was originally characterised
for its insulinotropic properties but has more recently been recognised as an important
regulator of adipose tissue metabolism; GIP receptor (GIPR) signalling in adipocytes promotes
lipid storage under fed conditions and may modulate energy expenditure, and in the central
nervous system GIPR is expressed in the hypothalamus and ventral tegmental area, suggesting
roles in reward-related eating behaviour [@Holst2020GIP]. The synergistic combination of
GLP-1R and GIPR agonism, as achieved by tirzepatide, produces greater weight loss than
selective GLP-1R agonism alone — a finding with profound mechanistic implications. Peptide YY
(PYY), co-secreted with GLP-1 from L-cells, acts on Y2 receptors in the ARC to inhibit
NPY/AgRP neurons and thereby suppress appetite. Cholecystokinin (CCK), released from
I-cells of the duodenum and jejunum in response to dietary fat and protein, activates CCK-A
receptors on vagal afferents and mediates short-term meal termination; unlike leptin and
insulin, CCK resistance does not appear to develop in obesity, making its pathway a continued
target of pharmacological interest [@Muller2022Antiobesity].

## Adipose Tissue as an Endocrine Organ

White adipose tissue (WAT) is no longer regarded as a passive energy reservoir but as a
metabolically active endocrine organ that secretes over 600 bioactive proteins collectively
termed adipokines. The contrast between visceral adipose tissue (VAT), concentrated in the
omental and mesenteric depots, and subcutaneous adipose tissue (SAT) is of central clinical
significance: VAT is characterised by greater lipolytic activity, higher macrophage infiltration,
and proximity to the portal circulation, resulting in delivery of free fatty acids and
pro-inflammatory cytokines directly to the liver, whereas SAT acts as a relatively protective
buffer depot with lower inflammatory tone [@Bluher2019Obesity; @Fasshauer2015Adipokines].
Leptin, the archetypal adipokine, is produced in direct proportion to adipocyte lipid content
and fat mass, yet fails functionally in the obese hypothalamus as described above. Adiponectin,
encoded by *ADIPOQ*, exhibits the opposite pattern: its circulating levels fall progressively
with increasing adiposity and insulin resistance, a paradox partly explained by the fact that
adiponectin has insulin-sensitising and anti-inflammatory properties — signalling through
AdipoR1 and AdipoR2 receptors to activate AMPK and PPAR-α pathways — that are lost when
adiponectin secretion is impaired. Resistin, interleukin-6 (IL-6), and tumour necrosis
factor-α (TNFα) are pro-inflammatory adipokines that increase with visceral adiposity; TNFα
impairs insulin signalling through serine phosphorylation of insulin receptor substrate-1
(IRS-1), contributing to peripheral insulin resistance and a chronic low-grade inflammatory
state that further drives adipose tissue dysfunction and cardiometabolic risk [@Fasshauer2015Adipokines].

## The Gut Microbiome and Metabolic Crosstalk

A landmark contribution to understanding obesity pathophysiology came from @Turnbaugh2006Obesity,
who demonstrated in a germ-free mouse model that colonisation with caecal microbiota harvested
from obese donors produced a significantly greater increase in total body fat than colonisation
with microbiota from lean donors — without any difference in caloric intake — establishing a
causal role for the gut microbiome in energy harvest and fat deposition. Metagenomic studies
in human cohorts have consistently reported an elevated Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio in
individuals with obesity, although the mechanistic interpretation remains nuanced, as functional
gene capacity for polysaccharide fermentation appears more important than phylum-level
composition. The microbiome influences host energy metabolism through several interconnected
mechanisms: production of short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) — principally acetate, propionate,
and butyrate — from dietary fibre fermentation, which signal through G-protein-coupled receptors
GPR41 (FFAR3) and GPR43 (FFAR2) on colonocytes, enteroendocrine L-cells, and adipocytes,
stimulating PYY and GLP-1 secretion; bile acid biotransformation, whereby primary bile acids
undergo 7α-dehydroxylation by Clostridiales to yield secondary bile acids that activate
Takeda G-protein receptor 5 (TGR5) on L-cells, further stimulating GLP-1 release; and
regulation of intestinal permeability and endotoxaemia through the toll-like receptor 4
(TLR4)-lipopolysaccharide axis, which contributes to metabolic inflammation [@Turnbaugh2006Obesity].

## Genetic Architecture and Developmental Programming

The heritability of BMI is estimated at 40–70% from twin studies, reflecting both polygenic
and rare monogenic contributions. The fat mass and obesity-associated gene (*FTO*) represents
the most replicated common variant locus: the rs9939609 risk allele, present in approximately
16% of individuals of European ancestry, is associated with an average 1.5 kg increase in
body weight and a 0.4 kg/m² increment in BMI per allele, acting partly through a regulatory
role on *IRX3* and *IRX5* expression in adipocyte precursors that shifts the balance from
thermogenic beige adipocyte differentiation toward lipid-storing white adipocyte
differentiation [@Muller2022Antiobesity; @Bluher2019Obesity]. Beyond *FTO*, genome-wide
association studies have identified over 900 loci contributing to BMI variance. At the
monogenic extreme, complete leptin deficiency arising from homozygous *LEP* mutations produces
severe early-onset obesity that is fully reversible with recombinant leptin replacement — a
proof-of-concept demonstration of the leptin–melanocortin axis's centrality. Leptin receptor
(*LEPR*) mutations produce a phenotypically similar syndrome with additional hyperpituitarism.
Epigenetic mechanisms, including DNA methylation changes at developmental programming windows
— particularly gestational overnutrition and excess gestational weight gain — imprint
adipogenic gene expression patterns that persist through life, linking maternal metabolic
health to offspring obesity risk via mechanisms operating through the hypothalamic–pituitary–
adrenal (HPA) axis and altered glucocorticoid receptor methylation.

## Obesogenic Environmental Drivers

The biological predisposition to obesity is amplified by pervasive environmental exposures
that systematically disrupt homeostatic energy regulation. Ultra-processed foods, classified
under the NOVA system as industrially formulated products containing ingredients and additives
not used in domestic cooking, are independently associated with excess energy intake beyond
that explained by their nutrient profiles, driven partly by engineered hyperpalatability
operating through mesolimbic dopamine circuits and partly by rapid gastric transit that
attenuates post-meal GLP-1 and PYY secretion [@WilsonPetruk2023Obesity]. Sleep curtailment
to below seven hours per night reliably suppresses leptin and elevates acyl-ghrelin — the
orexigenic stomach-derived peptide — creating a hormonal milieu that increases appetite by an
estimated 500 kcal/day. Chronic psychosocial stress activates the HPA axis, elevating cortisol
and promoting preferential VAT deposition through glucocorticoid receptor-mediated lipid uptake
in visceral adipocytes. The built environment, characterised by food deserts, limited active
transport infrastructure, and advertising saturation of energy-dense products, structures
behavioural choices in ways that are effectively invisible to individual volition. Finally,
endocrine-disrupting chemicals including bisphenol A (BPA) and phthalates — found in food
packaging and consumer products — interfere with adipogenesis and thyroid hormone signalling,
contributing to the so-called "chemical obesogens" hypothesis [@Bluher2019Obesity].

## Pharmacotherapeutic Exploitation of Pathophysiological Pathways

The foregoing mechanistic landscape directly defines the target space for anti-obesity
pharmacotherapy. GLP-1R agonists such as semaglutide exploit the gut–brain satiety axis by
providing sustained, pharmacological-level GLP-1R stimulation that exceeds the amplitude and
duration achievable by endogenous post-prandial secretion, thereby engaging both vagal afferent
and direct hypothalamic POMC-neuron pathways to reduce appetite and food reward [@Drucker2018Mechanisms;
@Wilding2021Once]. Tirzepatide adds GIPR co-agonism to this framework; the synergistic weight
loss produced — up to 22.5% of body weight at the 15 mg dose in SURMOUNT-1 — likely reflects
additive or supra-additive engagement of complementary hypothalamic and adipocyte-level circuits
[@Jastreboff2022Tirzepatide]. Naltrexone–bupropion targets the melanocortin pathway directly:
bupropion activates POMC neurons and increases α-MSH release, while naltrexone blocks
β-endorphin-mediated autoinhibitory feedback on POMC neurons, resulting in sustained
melanocortin tone [@Greenway2010Effect]. Orlistat operates peripherally, inhibiting intestinal
lipase to reduce dietary fat absorption by approximately 30%, increasing the luminal fat load
available to stimulate L-cell GLP-1 secretion as a secondary benefit. Bariatric surgery
exploits multiple overlapping pathways simultaneously — caloric restriction, altered bile
acid–TGR5 signalling, microbiome remodelling, and dramatic post-prandial GLP-1 surges — that
together account for weight loss outcomes substantially exceeding those attributable to caloric
restriction alone [@Batterham2016Neuroendocrine]. The convergence of mechanistic understanding
thus frames pharmacotherapy not as a blunt metabolic suppressor but as a precision modulator
of the specific neuroendocrine and peripheral circuits whose dysregulation drives the
pathophysiology of obesity.
